source: ASME B31.3 Table A-1 material groupings (metallic) and Chapter VII (non-metallic); ASTM and ISO product specifications. Allowable stress values are NOT included - see note.
note: Material library, PIPE group only. Hierarchy: group -> spec -> grade -> product form. Every numeric property carries verified:false until checked against a purchased copy of the standard, and unverified values must not be used in a calculation. Allowable stress (S) tables are deliberately absent: they are copyrighted and a wrong value silently corrupts a wall-thickness calculation. They are loaded separately once someone transcribes them from the standard.

conventions.storage: MTO rows store the strings group/spec/grade/productForm, never an array index.
conventions.zeroGrades: A spec may have an empty grades array. The UI disables the grade column; it does not show an empty dropdown.
conventions.productForm: Chosen in a fourth dropdown after the grade, because one spec can be supplied in several forms with different weld joint quality factors.
conventions.weldJointQualityFactor: Ew per ASME B31.3 Table A-1B. Seamless 1.00, ERW 0.85, EFW without RT 0.80, EFW with 100% RT 1.00, furnace butt welded 0.60.
conventions.nonMetallic: A non-metallic product form carries weldJointQualityFactor null, because ASME B31.3 Chapter VII designs it from a hydrostatic design basis rather than from S x E x W. Route on group.metallic BEFORE asking for a factor.
conventions.surfaceCondition: Offered only where a spec declares more than one, exactly like grades. Galvanising is orthogonal to the product form: A53 Type S, E and F can each be black or hot-dip zinc coated.
conventions.pressureRating: NOT held here. A flange rating (150#, 300#, ...) is a property of the COMPONENT under ASME B16.5/B16.47, not of the material, and piping_classes.pressure_rating already carries it. A105 is A105 whether the flange is 150# or 1500#.
conventions.family: A182 covers two ASTM tables - ferritic/martensitic F-grades and austenitic F3xx. They are one purchasable specification, so they are one spec here, with the family recorded as a grade property for filtering and for the welding rules that depend on it.
conventions.fittingProductForm: A403 class WP-S / WP-W / WP-WX and A815 WP-S / WP-W distinguish seamless from welded and from welded-plus-full-radiography. That is the PRODUCT FORM axis, not classOrType: putting it in the class would create two parallel axes for one fact and break the Ew lookup, exactly as folding A53 Type S/E/F into the grade would have.
conventions.castingQualityFactor: A cast product form carries weldJointQualityFactor 1.0 because there is no longitudinal seam to discount. That is NOT the whole story: ASME B31.3 para 302.3.3 applies a separate CASTING QUALITY FACTOR Ec, which depends on the examination the casting received and is not held in this pack. Do not read Ew=1.0 on a casting as 'no derating applies'.
conventions.valveTrim: A valve is the second ASSEMBLED component. An API trim number is ONE designation implying several machined parts, exactly as a spiral wound gasket is one catalogue item implying four materials, so it is a GRADE whose constituents are properties. A valve needs TWO answers - a BODY material from the cascade and a TRIM from its own selector - which is why VALVE_TRIM has no componentTypes: claiming ['VALVE'] would let the cascade offer 'Trim 8' where 'A216 WCB' belongs and leave the valve bodyless.
conventions.bolting: Bolting is its own component type (BOLT, NUT), NOT derived from the flanges. Projects order fasteners with an allowance over the calculated need, so deriving the quantity from the flange count would understate the take-off. The system must instead CHECK that the bolts and nuts entered are not FEWER than the flanges require, and that the diameters and lengths suit them - a reconciliation, not a derivation.
conventions.boltingHardness: maxHardness is the NACE MR0175 / ISO 15156 ceiling for sour service, and is why B7M and L7M exist as separate grades from B7 and L7: same alloy, lower hardness, lower strength. Recorded now because getting it wrong at incoming inspection is a sulphide stress cracking failure later.
conventions.noProvenanceOfTheMaterial: A material is recorded as WHAT IT IS, never as what it used to be. A welded pipe is rolled from plate, but 'ASTM A672 B60' already names the acceptance the finished pipe must meet, and the plate specification it was rolled from adds nothing a requisition, an inspection or a wall thickness calculation can act on. It was carried as free text on 42 grades and has been removed. Do not reintroduce it, here or anywhere else: the mill certificate is where a heat's history lives, and that belongs to the LOT, not to the library. The same reasoning is why the library holds no 'made from' link on fittings.
conventions.plateHasNoWeldJointFactor: PLATE carries Ew 1.0 for exactly the reason CAST and FORGED do: Ew derates a LONGITUDINAL SEAM and a flat plate has none, so there is nothing to derate. It does NOT mean the plate is as good as seamless in every sense - it means the seam term does not apply. When the plate is rolled into pipe the real factor appears, and it belongs to the pipe spec (A671/A672/A691, EFW 0.80 or EFW_RT 1.00), never to the plate. null is reserved for forms designed on a different basis entirely, such as the non-metallic route.
conventions.plateNormalisedCondition: A516 Gr 70 and A516 Gr 70N are the same specification and grade in two supply conditions, not two grades - which is why supplyCondition is a property and not part of the grade code. Normalising is what buys the low-temperature toughness, so a line blank ordered as A516 70 when the datasheet said normalised is a real incoming-inspection rejection.
conventions.structuralIsNotPressureRetaining: Structural plate lives in PLATE_STRUCTURAL, which supplies NO component types at all. Being in the library means a requisition can name it; it does not mean a pressure part may be cut from it. Every grade carries pressureRetaining false and the validator refuses to let such a spec sit in a group that supplies a pressure-retaining component. The first draft of the plate group put A283 next to A516 and the rule caught it - the cascade would have offered structural plate for a line blank.
conventions.assembledComponents: (SUPERSEDED - both halves are now built. See gasketConstituents and valveTrim.) GASKET and VALVE are not single-material components and the four-step cascade cannot describe them honestly. A spiral wound gasket has a winding, a filler and up to two rings; a valve has a body and a trim. Neither is really N materials, though: a vendor sells 'CG 316/graphite/CS' as one catalogue item and API 600 Trim 8 is one designation that implies a stem and a seat. The answer is expected to be a CONFIGURATION that references materials, not extra parallel dropdowns - and gasket style and trim number are the same shape of problem, so they will be solved together. Until then GASKET is deliberately unclaimed by any group and a valve carries its body material only. Do not half-solve one of them.
conventions.gasketConstituents: A gasket is the first ASSEMBLED component in this library: a spiral wound gasket has a metal winding, a non-metallic filler and up to two rings, and a vendor sells that whole combination as ONE catalogue item. So the grade is the catalogue item - 'CGI, 316 winding, graphite filler, CS outer ring' - and the constituents are recorded as properties of it, NOT as extra steps in the cascade. The cascade stays four steps deep for every component in the system. Constituents that name a metal MUST resolve against a grade this library actually holds (validator rule 20), the same discipline as wroughtEquivalent on the castings - which caught a genuine error in its author's data the first time it ran.
conventions.gasketOuterRingCorrodes: outerRingMaterial is recorded separately from windingMaterial because they are routinely different and the difference is a real failure: a carbon steel centring ring on a 316 winding is the standard, cheapest build, and in a chloride or marine service the ring corrodes away and the gasket loses its centring while the winding is untouched. A library that recorded only 'spiral wound 316' could not see that coming.
conventions.gasketFacing: permittedFacings is recorded now and VALIDATED LATER, deliberately - this round is materials only. A ring joint gasket seats only in an RTJ groove, a full-face gasket only on a flat face, and a spiral wound one on RF or FF. ports.facing and equipment_nozzles.facing already exist (RF/FF/RTJ) and PortCompatibility already warns on a facing mismatch between two ports, so the hook is there when someone wires it up. Same staging as the bolting round: get the reference right first, then the check.
conventions.gasketIsNotPressureRated: A gasket has no pressure rating of its own - it is rated by the JOINT it sits in, and the rating lives on piping_classes.pressure_rating exactly as for every other component. What a gasket does carry is a temperature ceiling from its filler: PTFE gives up around 260 C while graphite holds to 650 C, and that ceiling, not the flange class, is what fails first.
conventions.pressureDesignedGroups: metallic answers 'is this steel?'; pressureDesigned answers 'is this sized by the B31.3 wall thickness formula?'. For every group but one the two coincide, which is why the library conflated them until the gasket group arrived. A spiral wound gasket is unquestionably metallic and has no wall, no allowable stress and no weld joint quality factor - it is sized by the flange it seats in. Rules that ask about Ew and about surface condition therefore key on pressureDesigned, not on metallic. Splitting the two is what let the gasket group exist without weakening the guard that stops the metallic formula being run on GRE pipe. PIPE_NONMETALLIC is pressureDesigned false as well, and for a reason worth stating: GRE and PE ARE pressure-retaining, but B31.3 Chapter VII rates them from a qualified hydrostatic basis, not from S x E x W. The flag means 'sized by the metallic formula', so it is false for them too. Two groups reach false by different routes - a gasket has no pressure boundary at all, GRE has one that is rated differently.
conventions.reachedBy: Every group states HOW a user arrives at it, because 'no component types' had quietly come to mean 'structural' and that was only ever true of one group. CASCADE is the four-step material dropdown. CONSTITUENT means the group is never chosen directly and is only ever named by another grade's constituent property (BAR: nobody puts 'A276 410' on a valve line of an MTO, but trim 1 names it). TRIM is a selector alongside the body material. REQUISITION_ONLY is nameable on a requisition but supplies no component (PLATE_STRUCTURAL). The validator enforces the flag both ways: a group with component types must say CASCADE, and a CONSTITUENT group that nothing names is dead weight and fails (rule 23).
conventions.trimHardfacing: A hardfaced seat is a WELD OVERLAY - Stellite 6 is a cobalt-chromium alloy to AMS 5894, not an ASTM product specification - so it is deliberately exempt from the constituent-resolution rule: there is nothing in this library for it to resolve to and inventing a spec would be worse than the exemption. But an exemption with nothing in return is how free text creeps back, so rule 25 charges for it: any trim with a hardfaced OR hardened seat must state a minimum seat hardness. Hardness is the only property of an overlay a receiving inspector can actually measure - 350 HB for a Stellite overlay, 750 HB for hardened 13Cr - and it is what the ITP row for incoming valves will check.
conventions.trimIsNotATemperatureRating: A trim number constrains the valve but does not rate it. Trim 8 is commonly quoted as good to about 454 C; that is the SEAT overlay's limit, not the valve's, and the body material and the B16.34 rating still govern. The same discipline as the gasket: the constituent that gives up first sets the ceiling, and no rating is stored on a material.
conventions.barHasNoSeam: BAR carries Ew 1.0 for the reason PLATE, FORGED and CAST do - the weld joint quality factor derates a LONGITUDINAL SEAM and a bar has none. A276 and A182 hold the same 13Cr alloy; the difference is the product form, and a valve stem is machined from bar. Resolving trim to A182 F6a would have named the wrong form on the requisition even though the metal is right.
conventions.copperHasNoFamily: The copper nickels in B151 carry no family property, the same call the gasket round made for rubber. 'family' is a metallurgical axis - ferritic, austenitic, duplex, martensitic, nickel - and a copper alloy has no place on it. Absent is the honest answer; widening the enum would corrupt the axis for every grade that does sit on it.
conventions.trimBelongsToOneValveType: THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERED. API 600 is 'Steel Gate Valves - Flanged and Butt-welding Ends, Bolted Bonnets': it covers GATE VALVES AND NOTHING ELSE. Its trim chart is nonetheless quoted across the industry for every valve on a datasheet, and the first version of this group repeated that error - a single API600 spec with no valve-type axis, so all 20 gate trims were offered for ball, butterfly and check valves too. The user caught it. Each valve type now has its own standard: API 600 gate, API 623 globe, API 594 check, API 608 ball, API 609 butterfly, API 599 plug. appliesToValveTypes carries the claim, rule 26 refuses two standards claiming one type, and trimsFor() is the only honest way to ask. NEEDLE and DIAPHRAGM are deliberately uncovered: null is a real answer.
conventions.trimPartsAreNotUniversal: The four parts of the API 600 chart - seat, disc, backseat, stem - are the parts a RISING STEM valve has, not the parts a valve has. A ball valve has a BALL and no backseat; a check valve has a HINGE PIN and no stem at all, because it has no actuator and nothing to seal a stem against; a plug valve has a PLUG. requiredParts is therefore per specification and rule 24 reads it from there. The first version hard-coded the gate parts and would have demanded a backseat from a ball valve - inventing a component that does not exist, which is worse than omitting one that does.
conventions.trimSoftSeat: A ball, butterfly or sleeved plug valve normally seals on a POLYMER, not on steel, and the polymer is what fails first - the same truth the gasket round found about fillers. Virgin PTFE 204 C, reinforced PTFE 232 C, PEEK 260 C, EPDM 120 C, NBR 100 C. Above those the seat creeps out of its pocket while the body is untroubled, so rule 27 requires a ceiling on any polymer seat and rule 28 refuses a trim that claims to be both soft seated and hardfaced - they are opposite answers to one question, and a grade claiming both is one chart pasted into another.
conventions.globeStemDiameter: API 623 (2013) was the first globe valve standard; before it people quoted API 600 wall thicknesses for globe valves because nothing else existed. Its trim chart mirrors API 600, but it adds a minimum STEM DIAMETER: a globe valve needs far more closing thrust than a gate valve, and an austenitic stem (304, 316, 347) is weaker than 410, so it must be larger or it buckles. Recorded as requiresOversizeStem - the actual diameters are dimensional data this pack does not hold.

stemDiameterRule.text: The minimum stem diameter is given by Table 5 and applies to the packing contact area and to the major diameter of the trapezoidal thread. "The actual stem diameter shall take into account the valve design details and THE STEM MATERIAL STRENGTH CHARACTERISTICS", and the stem strength bounds the maximum input force from the handwheel or gearbox per MSS SP-91.
stemDiameterRule.replacesAnInventedProperty: The chart this spec grew from carried a per-trim boolean, requiresOversizeStem, set on the austenitic trims. API 623 says no such thing. It states a DESIGN OBLIGATION on the manufacturer - account for the stem material strength - not a per-trim-number flag a transcriber could tick. The boolean was a plausible simplification of a real rule, which is the hardest kind of invention to spot.

specs._note: Twelve numbered trims read from API 594-2022 Table 4. The four codes this spec used to hold - 13CR, STL, 316, MONEL - were invented: API 594 numbers its trims like every other API valve standard, and no sheet anywhere says "trim STL". A check valve has a SEATING SURFACE and a HINGE PIN, and no stem and no backseat, which is why requiredParts is two and not four.
specs.hardnessNotSpecified: API 594-2022 states no seat hardness anywhere - the words hardness, HB and Brinell do not appear in the document. The absence is the standard’s answer, and a figure borrowed from a gate-valve chart would be an inspection criterion nobody wrote.

noTrimNumberSystem.PLUG: API 599-2025 has NO trim number table. Unlike API 600, 623 and 594, it never numbers a trim: clause 6 gives the shell from ASME B16.34 or a ductile iron from B16.42, and leaves seat, sleeve and plug facing to be agreed on the purchase order. The two codes this library held for plug valves - PTFE-SLV and MTL - were a vocabulary for a chart that does not exist. Offering them invited a transcriber to pick a trim number no plug valve has.
